needs.have_it_when: You can name the one person whose yes counts.

needs.name: One real case from your own work, picked because it is hard

needs.have_it_when: You picked the one that has gone wrong before.

needs.name: A kind of work you have not done this way before

needs.name: A pile of raw material, as it came
needs.why: Everything is listed, sorted and chosen from it.
needs.have_it_when: It is all in one place an agent can read.

ways.says: Put it in one folder before sorting any of it.

needs.name: A task with an input, an output and a check
needs.why: Only a task with a check can be handed down safely.
needs.have_it_when: You can say how you will know it was done right.

ways.says: Write the check before the brief.

needs.name: An ad account you may work in
needs.why: The pieces run there. Not every role may write.
needs.have_it_when: A paused upload goes in under your own sign-in.

ways.says: Ask the account's owner for the role, then check it with one first try.
Work with what you have. On the run one kind of upload was refused, and the videos went in by hand.

needs.name: Finished video ads
needs.why: Everything after this is about finished pieces.
needs.have_it_when: Each plays from start to end, and someone has watched it whole.

needs.name: A connection that lets your agent read and write the ad account

needs.have_it_when: It reads the account back to you, and one paused draft goes in.

ways.says: The platform's own connector. On the run it read and wrote, and could not upload files.
Let the connector fetch each video from a link.

needs.name: An owner that admits answers against the current question
needs.why: Checking in the browser before submitting cannot prevent the question changing in between.
needs.have_it_when: A disposable test proves atomic admission, refusal of changed or closed questions, duplicate handling and a retained owner journal you can read back.

ways.says: Use the workflow engine's native atomic answer operation. The desk proved it with a disposable real-engine ask and duplicate refusal.

needs.name: A person who watches and listens
needs.why: A transcript cannot tell a good take from a flat one.
needs.have_it_when: Someone will watch the whole reel and say yes or no to each line.

needs.name: The best take of each line you said, approved
needs.why: Ads are written from lines that are already right.
needs.have_it_when: Each line has one take, and you have said yes to it.

ways.says: Bring clips an editor already cut.

needs.name: The offer, the story, the figures that may be said, and the rules
needs.why: The cutting, the writing and the checking all work from it.
needs.have_it_when: An agent can answer from it who it is for, what they get and why this person. Each figure is cleared or held. What must never be seen or said is listed.

ways.says: Point the agent at what the person has already written.

needs.name: What you will spend a day
needs.why: Where things run and how many depend on it.
needs.have_it_when: You can say one number, and whose money it is.

ways.says: Say it in the same sitting as the goal.

needs.name: Things you can make the first time someone asks
needs.why: A promise only works if the thing behind it can be made.
needs.have_it_when: Each has a name beside it: who makes it, and how long it takes.

ways.says: List what the person already has or can write when asked.

needs.name: An agent that can read your files and run commands
needs.why: It writes and runs the scripts for each step, and reads what they print.
needs.have_it_when: It can list a folder you name and run a command in it.

ways.says: Claude Code, in an app that keeps its threads, with cheaper models taking narrow tasks. Any agent that passes the test will do.

needs.name: A script: a list of lines in, a finished video out
needs.why: Once lines are approved, a new piece is a list.
needs.have_it_when: One list gives one video that passes its checks.

ways.says: Have the agent write one on ffmpeg. The run's took about half a second for each second of video.

needs.name: The conversations that follow
needs.why: They are said in someone's name.
needs.have_it_when: The person has read each one and corrected it.

ways.says: Draft them, then show the person.

needs.name: Somewhere for a lead to go

needs.have_it_when: You open it on your phone, and a test reaches a person.

ways.says: A page with an application and a way to book.

needs.name: Room to work

needs.have_it_when: About ten times the size of the footage is free on the disk you will work on. An external one is safer.

ways.says: An external drive. The run had about 200 GB free.

needs.name: Videos of someone talking to camera
needs.why: Everything is cut from these. A shared album or a link is not something an agent can cut.
needs.have_it_when: There is a folder where every file plays in a tool that reads video, and the count matches what whoever filmed them says they shot.

ways.says: Download the shared album from its website in a browser.
Ask whoever shot them for originals, not a messaging app's copies.

needs.name: What you want at the end
needs.why: It decides what is worth making.
needs.have_it_when: You can say it in one sentence, with how you would know it happened.

ways.says: Say it before anything is made, and write it down.

needs.name: A list of many things to make the same way
needs.why: The first is picked from it and the rest are made from it.
needs.have_it_when: Each has a row, and the rows are alike.

ways.says: Write the list before making the first.

needs.name: ffmpeg and ffprobe, built to draw text
needs.why: Every measure, cut and render goes through them.
needs.have_it_when: ffmpeg lists a drawtext filter.

ways.says: Ask your agent to install it. A plain build may not draw text; the run needed a second build.

needs.name: Who says yes or no, and who is in the videos
needs.why: Some answers are only theirs.
needs.have_it_when: You can name each, and what each may decide. They may be the same person.

ways.says: Name them at the start.

needs.name: What to film next
needs.why: The person has to know what to film.
needs.have_it_when: Each has the words to say and why.

ways.says: List what the set needs and nobody said.

needs.name: Where each ad runs, what it asks for, and the money
needs.why: Nothing is switched on out of order.
needs.have_it_when: Each piece has a place, one ask and its money, and the order is written.

ways.says: Draw it with the finished pieces in front of you.

needs.name: A private page they can sign in to
needs.why: A page that holds only what needs them can be answered in a minute.
needs.have_it_when: They open it on their own phone.

ways.says: Build it from the files that already hold the work. Built once, and only run on one machine.

needs.name: Formats that have worked for offers like this

needs.have_it_when: Each format has one worked example.

ways.says: Take them from someone who has run similar offers.

needs.name: A way to reach the person that you have agreed on

needs.have_it_when: You have said which way, and they have used it.

ways.says: The messages you already send each other.
Their own email and a sign-in.

needs.have_it_when: You tried to change something through it, and it refused.

needs.have_it_when: Your agent can open the record and read the number back.

ways.says: Read the ad account through its connector.

needs.why: The number you judge by is what it cost to get what you wanted.
needs.have_it_when: One test click shows up under the right name.

ways.says: Open one ad's link with its tag, and look for it before judging anything by it.

needs.name: The client's notes, and the fixes
needs.why: Words about a person follow what they said back.
needs.have_it_when: Each note is fixed, or has the reason it was not.

ways.says: Show them, and write down what they say.

needs.name: How the person handles someone who gets in touch
needs.why: What is promised has to be what happens.
needs.have_it_when: They have read your version and corrected it.

ways.says: Outline it from what they said on camera, marking every guess.
A two-minute video of them walking through it, then a correction.

needs.name: What the person has already said and written
needs.why: The brief is made from their words.
needs.have_it_when: There is a folder your agent can read, with at least one thing in it they said or wrote themselves.

ways.says: Export their notes and documents.
Record them answering for twenty minutes.

needs.name: A first pass at where each piece runs and what it asks for
needs.why: A piece is cut for where it runs and what it asks.
needs.have_it_when: Every kind of piece has a place and one thing it asks for.

ways.says: Work it out in the same sitting as the set.

needs.name: A person who answers every message within minutes
needs.why: A promise unanswered is worse than none.
needs.have_it_when: You can name who, on which surfaces, in what hours.

ways.says: Name them before the first ad asks for a message.

needs.name: Something finished that is meant to go out
needs.why: It is what gets put in place.
needs.have_it_when: It is done, and someone has looked at it whole.

ways.says: Finish one before staging any.

needs.have_it_when: You can open it, and its owner has said what you may do there.

needs.name: The instructions your agents already read
needs.why: A rule is written where it will be read.
needs.have_it_when: You know which file each kind of agent loads.

ways.says: List the instruction files and the skills.

needs.name: The exact question and the consequence of answering it
needs.why: An answer without its question and version can be applied to something the person never saw.
needs.have_it_when: The record contains question identity and version, readable context, allowed responses and what each response does.

ways.says: Read the current question from its owning workflow or graph, including the source artifact the person is deciding about.

needs.name: Every option you have for the job
needs.why: Only what is on the list gets tried.
needs.have_it_when: Each is installed or reachable, and you could run it today.

ways.says: List what is on the machine and which keys you hold.

needs.have_it_when: One take comes back with every word timed, and the last word ends inside the take.

One on your machine, which keeps the sound there.

needs.name: What each worker costs and what it is good for
needs.why: The cheapest that can do a task is chosen from it.
needs.have_it_when: There is a price and a note for each one you can call.

ways.says: Read the providers' price pages.

needs.name: A word people send you, and what they get for it

needs.have_it_when: Each word has one promise you can keep, and the person has corrected it.

courses.title: The 2027 MasterClass
courses.tagline: One new company, from the first message to live, with every move explained.
courses.about: One long film. A new business goes from nothing to a live site, live ads, tracking, booking and follow-up in one sitting, and you watch every move with the reason for it. The first five minutes are enough to start. The rest is the same ground at depth.

courses.title: The Curriculum
courses.tagline: Fifteen short lessons, from asking AI questions to handing over results.
courses.about: The craft of directing agents, one distinction at a time: what to hand over, how to say what you want, the standard, the limits, and how to make all of it compound.

courses.title: The Runbooks
courses.tagline: One result at a time: what you get, and the few things only you can give.
courses.about: A page that takes bookings. Ads live in your own account. Every step measured. Follow-up that sends itself. Each one built for real, with what it asked of the owner.

parts.title: Put them to work
parts.shift: From asking to having it done
parts.intro: Get your own agents onto your own computer, let them learn the business from its records, and have one real thing done before the day is over.
parts.crossed: Your agents did real work in your business, and you hold a picture of it you could not have written yourself.

parts.title: Hand over the result
parts.intro: The six things a result needs from you before it can run without you: its size, what you want, the standard, the limits, room to run in parallel, and your judgment at the end.
parts.crossed: You handed over a result with a score and limits. It ran without you, and you judged what came back.

parts.title: Make it compound
parts.intro: Work that is done once is spent. Work that leaves a better way of working behind it compounds. This is the part almost nobody teaches.
parts.crossed: Your agents got better at something because of how you run them, and you did none of that work yourself.

lessons.title: What good looks like
lessons.promise: See the gap between asking AI questions and having agents do the work.
idea: Most people use AI like a very fast intern they supervise word by word. Ask, read, copy, paste, fix, ask again. The work still passes through their own hands, so it can only go as fast as they can.

A small number of owners work another way. Their agents run on their own computer, inside their own files and accounts, on real work, several at a time. The owner says what is wanted, gives a yes where one is needed, and judges what comes back.
The difference is not a cleverer prompt. It is where the agent works and how much you hand it. An agent in a chat window can only talk. An agent on your computer can do.
So the first step is small and practical: one free app, signed in with the plan you already pay for. You do not need to become technical, and you never write code.
lessons.tape: One person and his agents started a new company from nothing: the site, the ads, the tracking, the booking page, the follow-up email. He sent 16 messages, about 1,100 words in all. The first campaign was live 1 hour 41 minutes after the first one.
lessons.yours: A computer, a $20 Claude or ChatGPT plan, and about an hour.
lessons.theirs: Every step of the install, given to you one at a time, waiting for you after each.
lessons.back: Claude or ChatGPT walks you through installing T3 Code, the free app your agents will work in, and signing in with your plan. It waits for you after each step.
judge: T3 Code is open on your computer.
You signed in with the plan you already pay for. You bought nothing new.
An agent answered you inside the app, not in a browser tab.
lessons.done: An agent has answered you from inside T3 Code on your own computer.

lessons.title: Let them learn your business
lessons.promise: Give your agents the one thing every good hire needs first.
idea: A new senior hire is useless for the first week, however good they are. They do not know who you serve, how the money moves, or what you tried last year. Every chat you have ever opened with an AI started on that same first day.

So the first thing your agents build is a written picture of your business that they and you both work from: who you serve, where the money comes from, where it gets stuck, and what is holding it back.
It lives in a folder on your computer, not inside one conversation. Every agent you start after this reads it first, so you never brief from zero again.
Answer its questions the way you would answer a sharp new partner. Short and true beats long and polished.
lessons.yours: Straight answers to a handful of questions, and anything you can point it at: a site, a deck, a spreadsheet.
lessons.theirs: The questions, the reading, and the written picture.

say.text: read agenticu.surf and set me up

lessons.back: A short set of questions, then a page about your business in plain words, saved where every later agent will find it.
judge: You would hand this page to a new senior hire on their first day.
It says at least one thing you did not tell it.
It names what it does not know yet, and does not guess.
lessons.done: A written picture of your business exists on your computer, and you corrected it once.

lessons.title: Open one door
lessons.promise: Let your agents read the business itself, not only your account of it.
idea: An agent that has only heard you describe the business knows your opinion of it. Useful, and exactly what your last consultant had.
An agent that has read your records knows the business. Payments, bookings, the ad account, the books: the truth is in there, and it often disagrees with what everyone in the building believes.
So open one door. Read-only, to the one system that would say the most. You sign in yourself, and your agent never needs your password typed into the chat.
This is the step that separates a pleasant conversation from an agent that can be trusted with work.
lessons.yours: The door. Only you can open it, and you choose which one.
lessons.theirs: Knowing which access to ask for, reading everything behind it, and saying where each number came from.

say.text: Pick the one system that would tell you the most about where my money comes from and where it gets stuck. Tell me exactly what read-only access you need and walk me through giving it. Then read it, and tell me what the records show that I did not tell you. Put numbers on it and say where each one came from.

lessons.back: One clear request for access. Then findings, each with a number and its source, added to the picture of your business.
judge: Every number says where it was read from.
At least one finding surprised you or disagreed with what you said.
Nothing in that system was changed.
lessons.done: The picture of your business carries a number your agents read from your own records.

lessons.title: Get one real thing done
lessons.promise: End the first day with finished work you did not do.
idea: Most owners are hard at work on the wrong problem. In any business, at any moment, one thing is capping it. Work on anything else is motion.

Now that your agents can see the records, ask them what that one thing is, and make them show the evidence. You know the business better than they do. They have read more of its data this week than you have this year. Argue until you agree.
Then have them do one piece of work on it today. Small enough to finish, real enough to matter: the follow-up nobody sent, the page that was never built, the report nobody had time to pull.
They stop before anything is sent, spent or published. That line is yours. Hold it now and you can move it later, on purpose.
lessons.yours: Agreeing what is in the way, and the yes before anything leaves the building.
lessons.theirs: The evidence, the proposal, and the work.

say.text: From what you now know, what is the one thing capping this business right now? Show me the evidence. Then propose one piece of work you can finish today that moves it, tell me what you need from me, and stop before anything is sent, spent or published.

lessons.back: The constraint with its evidence, one proposal, a short list of what it needs from you, then finished work waiting at your line.
judge: The evidence comes from your records, not from general advice.
The work is finished, not outlined.
It stopped where you told it to.
lessons.done: A finished piece of work exists in your business that you did not do.

lessons.title: Task, project, result
lessons.promise: Learn the three sizes of what you can hand over, and why you have been using the smallest.
idea: There are three sizes of thing you can hand to anyone. A task: write this email. A project: launch this campaign. A result: get me booked calls.
Each step up, you say less about how and more about what good is. Nobody tells a head of sales which emails to write. You tell them the number and the rules, and you look at the number.
Chat taught everyone to hand AI tasks, because a chat window can do nothing else. Your agents can hold a project now, and with what the next five lessons give them, a result.
You already run people this way. Nothing here is new to you except who is on the other end.
lessons.tape: The first message that Saturday was a few lines: a new site, a way to book a call, then ads. Thirteen specialist jobs followed from it.
lessons.yours: Deciding the size. You are the only one who can hand over a result.
lessons.theirs: Working out the projects and tasks underneath it.

say.text: Here is something I have been handing you as tasks: [the work]. Restate it as a result: what I actually want, how we would know we have it, and the projects that sit under it. Then tell me what you would need from me to own all of it.

lessons.back: The result in one sentence, how it would be measured, the projects under it, and what it needs from you.
judge: The result is something a customer or your bank account would notice.
You could check it without reading any of the work.
The list of what it needs from you is short and specific.
lessons.done: One thing you used to hand over as tasks is written down as a result.

lessons.title: Say what you want
lessons.promise: Brief an agent the way you would brief your best hire.
idea: When work comes back wrong, the usual cause is not a weak agent. It is that what you wanted never left your head.

A good brief has four parts and no steps. The result. Who it is for. What would make it a failure. Why it matters now. Give the reason and your agents make a hundred small decisions the way you would have.

Then make them say it back before they start. You will hear what you actually said, which is rarely what you meant. Correcting a say-back takes one message. Correcting finished work means doing it over.
Tell them to ask you only what they cannot find out themselves. A question they could have answered from your own files is your time spent on their work.
lessons.yours: What you want and why. Nobody else has it.
lessons.theirs: Saying it back, finding what can be found, and asking only for the rest.

say.text: I want [the result]. Before you start, say it back to me in your own words: the result, who it is for, what would make it a failure, and what you are assuming. Ask me only what you cannot find out yourself.

lessons.back: Your intent in their words, a list of assumptions, and a small number of questions that only you could answer.
judge: The say-back contains something you would have corrected later.
Every question is one only you could answer.
It has not started the work yet.
lessons.done: An agent said your intent back to you, and you corrected it before any work began.

lessons.title: The standard and the score
lessons.promise: Make good something your agents can check without you.
idea: Without a standard, an agent marks its own homework, and everything comes back done. This is the part of handing over a result that most people skip, and it is the hard one.
A standard is anything checkable: an example of good work, a test that passes or fails, a number read from a place neither of you can argue with.
The score is the standard kept over time. Booked calls this week. Cost of each one. Agree where it is read from and how often, and what counts as good, fine and bad.
Decide the stop rules before you start, while you are calm. What number means carry on, and what number means stop and come to me.
lessons.tape: The rules for when to stop an ad were written down before the campaign was published, not after the first bad day.
lessons.yours: What good is. Your taste, your margins and your customers decide it.
lessons.theirs: Proposing how to measure it, then keeping the score without being asked.

say.text: For [the result], propose how we will score it: the number, where it is read from, how often, and what counts as good, fine and bad. Show me one example of work that meets the standard and one that does not. I will correct you. After that, keep the score without my asking.

lessons.back: A proposed score with its source, two examples to react to, and after your correction, a number that keeps arriving.
judge: The number is read from your own records, not estimated.
You disagreed with at least one example, and the standard changed.
It says in advance what number would make it stop.
lessons.done: Your result has a score, read from your own records, that you agreed to.

lessons.title: The say
lessons.promise: Decide once what needs your yes, so you stop being the bottleneck.
idea: You have the say. The question is where you spend it. If every step waits for you, you have built a faster way to be interrupted.

Sort everything your agents might do into three piles. Do without asking. Ask me first. Never. Spending money, sending to a real person, publishing, deleting, and anything that cannot be undone start in ask first.

Then give standing yeses with limits. Pause any ad that loses more than this much, and tell me after. Reply to booking questions, but never quote a price. A limit is what makes a yes safe to give in advance.
Have it written where every agent of yours reads it. Rules that live in one conversation are forgotten by the next.
lessons.tape: The owner's hand was needed for a short list: the offer, the daily budget, the go to put the site live, and the go to publish the campaign. Thirteen follow-up emails were written and wired that night, and stayed in test mode until their words were approved.
lessons.yours: Every yes, every limit, every key.
lessons.theirs: Finding everything that needs one, proposing where the lines go, and keeping to them.

say.text: List everything in [the result] that spends money, sends something to a person, publishes, deletes, or cannot be undone. For each one propose: do without asking, ask me first, or never. Suggest a limit wherever a standing yes would be safe. Write what I agree to where every agent of mine will read it.

lessons.back: A sorted list with proposed limits, and after your edits, a short written set of rules in your business folder.
judge: It found something risky you had not thought of.
At least one thing moved to do without asking, with a limit.
A new agent, started tomorrow, would read the same rules.
lessons.done: Your standing yeses and limits are written down, and an agent acted inside one without asking.

lessons.title: Run more than one
lessons.promise: Stop working in a line. Have the pieces run at the same time.
idea: The slow part of any project with people is the waiting. The designer waits for the copy. Tracking waits for the page. Each brief is rewritten for the next person in the line.
Your agents do not have to work in a line. One holds the result and keeps the list. Under it, as many as the work needs run at once: one on the page, one on the research, one on the emails.
Your part gets smaller, not larger. You are not managing five conversations. You are reading one list: what is running, what is waiting on you, what is done.
This is the moment it stops feeling like software and starts feeling like a staff.
lessons.tape: While the campaign was being built, separate agents were researching the ad platform and setting up the email system. Thirteen specialist jobs were covered in one sitting, with no handoffs between people.
lessons.yours: One result, held in one place, and your attention only where it is asked for.
lessons.theirs: Splitting the work, running the pieces together, and keeping the list.

say.text: Break [the result] into the pieces that can run at the same time, and start an agent on each. Keep one list of what is running, what is waiting on me, and what is done. Bring me only what needs me.

lessons.back: A plan of parallel pieces, agents started on each, and one list you can read in a minute.
judge: More than one thing was moving at the same time.
Everything waiting on you was in one place.
You were not asked anything they could have settled themselves.
lessons.done: Several pieces of one result ran at once, and you were asked only for what needed you.

lessons.title: Judge what comes back
lessons.promise: Check a week of work in minutes, the way you inspect any operation you own.
idea: You cannot read everything your agents do, and you should not try. You do not read every email your team sends either. You inspect results.
Done is a claim. Ask for the proof instead: the page that loads, the number in the account, the test that ran and what it returned.
Ask what was not checked. The honest answer to that one question tells you more than any report, and it trains your agents to tell you the truth first.
Then decide like an owner. Accept it, send it back with one sentence about what is wrong, or change the standard because you have learned what you actually want.
lessons.yours: The judgment. Is this good, for this business, for these customers.
lessons.theirs: Putting the evidence in front of you, including what they did not check.

say.text: Do not tell me it is done. Show me: where I can see it for myself, the check you ran and what it returned, what you did not check, and what you would look at first if you were me.

lessons.back: A short page of evidence with links you can open, and a plain list of what is still unproven.
judge: You could verify the main claim yourself in under a minute.
It told you something that was not finished or not checked.
You accepted it or sent it back without reading the work itself.
lessons.done: You accepted or sent back a finished result from its evidence alone.

lessons.title: A, B, C
lessons.promise: Learn the three levels every company works on, and staff the two you have been skipping.
idea: A is the work: the campaign, the page, the report. B is improving how the work gets done: the checklist, the template, the lesson from last time. C is improving how the improving gets done: how lessons are found, written down and put to use.
Every company does all three. Most only staff A. B happens when someone has a quiet Friday, and C happens at an offsite once a year.

With agents, B and C cost almost nothing, because the one who did the work can write the lesson the minute the work is finished. But only if you ask. Left alone, agents do A forever, and start from zero every morning.
This is where the people far ahead of you are spending their attention. Their agents are not smarter than yours. Theirs have been improving every day for a year.
lessons.tape: While the company was being built, the agent stopped five times to write a note for next time: how it got through a sign-in, how it handed work to other agents, how it set up the address. Those five things are known before the next build starts.
lessons.yours: Asking for B and C, every time, until it is a habit your agents have without you.
lessons.theirs: Writing down what was learned, where the next agent will read it before starting.

say.text: For the work we just finished: what did you learn that would make the next run faster or better? Write each lesson as a standing instruction where the next agent will read it before it starts. Then show me what you wrote.

lessons.back: A short list of lessons, written into your business folder as instructions, not as a report to you.
judge: Each lesson is specific to your business, not general advice.
It is saved where a new agent would read it without being told.
You can name one thing the next run will not have to rediscover.
lessons.done: The same kind of work was done a second time, and it started from a written lesson.

lessons.title: Never explain twice
lessons.promise: Turn every correction you give into one you never give again.
idea: Every time you correct an agent, the correction goes one of two places. It fixes this piece of work and is gone. Or it changes the way the work is done, and stays.
The second costs one more sentence. Do not only fix this. Find what let it through, and change that.

Do it every time and your corrections stack up into a way of working that is yours: your standards, your tone, the things your customers care about, the mistakes your business has already paid for once.
That stack is the real asset. The models will be replaced every few months. What your agents know about how you want things done carries over to every one of them.
lessons.yours: Noticing what is wrong. Your eye is the source of every standard your agents will ever have.
lessons.theirs: Tracing the mistake to the instruction or the check that let it through, and changing that.

say.text: I just corrected you on [the mistake]. Do not only fix this one. Find where it came from, change the instruction or the check that let it through, and tell me what you changed so that no agent of mine makes it again.

lessons.back: The fixed work, the cause, and the exact line that was added or changed in your standing instructions.
judge: It changed a rule, not only the result.
The new rule would have caught this mistake.
It is short enough that an agent will actually follow it.
lessons.done: A correction you gave once did not have to be given a second time.

lessons.title: Keep the record
lessons.promise: Make everything your business does add to what it knows.
idea: Most of what a company learns is lost. It was said in a meeting, decided in a hallway, or it left with the person who knew it.
Your agents can keep the record as they work: what you asked for, what was decided and why, what was done, what it produced. In plain files, in your folder, readable by you.

The record is what lets a new agent pick up where the last one stopped. It is what lets you ask why you decided something in March and get the real answer. It is what you hand to the person who buys the business.
It also turns your work into something you can show. A night of real work, on the record, is the most convincing thing you will ever put in front of a customer.
lessons.tape: There was no camera running. The whole night was rebuilt afterwards, minute by minute, from the transcript of the session. Everything on this site about it comes from that record.
lessons.yours: Working where the record is kept, and reading it now and then.
lessons.theirs: Keeping it, without being asked, every time.

say.text: Set up a simple record for this business: what I asked for, what was decided and why, what was done, and what it produced. Keep it without being asked, in plain files I can read. Then show me yesterday from it.

lessons.back: A place in your business folder where the record lives, and yesterday told back to you from it.
judge: You can read it without help.
It has the why, not only the what.
A brand new agent, given only the record, could continue the work.
lessons.done: You asked what happened last week and why, and the answer came from the record.

lessons.title: What a staff does to you
lessons.promise: Guard against the four things that have always gone wrong for people who are well served.
idea: For most of history only rulers had a staff, and the oldest books of advice were written to them. They warn of the same four troubles every time. You now have a staff, so they are yours.
Flattery. Your agents are built to be agreeable. Left alone, they will tell you the plan is good. Ask for the case against, with evidence, before every decision that matters.

The servant who knows more than the master. Your agents will soon know parts of your business better than you. That is the point of having them, and it is only safe if you can still ask the question that shows whether the work is right. And softness: when everything is done for you, you lose the feel of the work. Keep your hands on the few things that are your craft.
Isolation. A staff that handles everything can stand between you and your customers. Stay where they are. No agent can tell you what the room felt like.
lessons.yours: Wanting the truth more than you want to be right.
lessons.theirs: Making the case against, and telling you what they know that you do not.

say.text: Tell me what I would not want to hear about [the decision]. Make the strongest case against it, with evidence from our own records. Then tell me what you know about this business that I do not seem to.

lessons.back: A case against your own decision, built from your own numbers, and a short list of things you had not been told.
judge: It disagreed with you plainly, and did not soften it.
The evidence was yours, not general.
You changed something, or you can say exactly why you did not.
lessons.done: Your agents told you something unwelcome, with evidence, and you acted on it.

lessons.title: What to hand over next
lessons.promise: Turn one result into a business that hands over more every month.
idea: You have now done the whole loop once. A result with a standard, limits and a record, which ran without you and got better the second time.
Everything after this is the same loop on a new part of the business. The only real question is the order.
Rank by what the business needs, not by what looks easiest to automate. What would bring in the most, or free the most of you, if it ran without you? Start there, even if it is hard.
This is also why the leader goes first. You cannot ask a company to work this way from a slide. Once you have done it yourself, you will know exactly what to ask of everyone else.
lessons.yours: The order. It is a decision about your business, and it is yours.
lessons.theirs: Finding the candidates, sizing each one, and saying what would have to be true first.

say.text: Using our record and what you know of this business, list the results that could be handed over next. Rank them by what each would bring in or free up. For each one tell me what you would need from me, and what would have to be true first.

lessons.back: A ranked list of results to hand over, each with what it needs from you and what it depends on.
judge: The ranking is argued from your numbers.
The first item is something that matters, not something that is easy.
You know what it needs from you this week.
lessons.done: You hold a ranked list of what to hand over next, and the first one is running.

runbooks.title: A picture of your business you both work from
runbooks.get: A written account of who you serve, where the money comes from, where it gets stuck and what is holding it back, with numbers read from your own records. Every agent you start reads it first.

asks.text: Straight answers to a short set of questions about the business.
Read-only access to the one system that says the most: payments, bookings, the ad account or the books.
Your agreement on what is in the way, before any work is done about it.

good: You would hand it to a new senior hire on day one.
Its main claim carries a number from your records, with the source.
It says what it does not know.
runbooks.say: read agenticu.surf and set me up

runbooks.title: A page that takes bookings
runbooks.get: A site for one offer, on your own address: the page, the application, the calendar, the confirmation, and the page for people who are not a fit.

asks.text: The offer: what you sell, to whom, for how much, and who you turn away.
Your domain, and the calendar or booking tool you already use.
The go to put it live on your address.

good: A stranger can book a call from their phone without help.
The booking lands in your real calendar.
People who are not a fit are told so kindly, and do not reach your calendar.
runbooks.say: Build me a page that takes bookings for [the offer]. Read the picture of my business first. Tell me what you need from me, show me a preview before anything goes on my address, and stop for my yes before it is live.
runbooks.night: A first version was up 16 minutes after the first message. The finished site was live on its own address at 52 minutes.

runbooks.title: Ads live in your own account
runbooks.get: A campaign in your ad account: the research, the plan with its stop rules, the ads themselves, and scripts for the videos only you can film.

asks.text: Your ad account. Sign in yourself in its browser window, including any code sent to your phone. Keep the code out of the chat.
The daily budget, and what a booked call is worth to you.
Photos of your real work, and yourself on camera for the videos.
The go to publish. Nothing spends before it.

good: The stop rules were agreed before the first dollar was spent.
Every ad points at a page that works on a phone.
You can see the campaign yourself, in your own account.
runbooks.say: Get ads live in my own ad account for [the offer]. Research what is working on the platform now, propose the plan and the rules for stopping an ad before we start, and make the first ads from my own photos. Tell me what only I can film. Publish nothing without my yes.
runbooks.night: Four ads were made from the business's own job photos, and the campaign was published 1 hour 41 minutes after the first message.

runbooks.title: Every step measured, from the ad to the deal
runbooks.get: One place that shows the whole path: who saw the ad, who clicked, who applied, who booked, who showed up, who bought. Read from the systems themselves.

asks.text: Your analytics, your ad account and your booking tool, read-only.
Tracking counts from the day it is installed. The first real answers take a few days of traffic.

good: You can follow one real person from the ad to the booking.
Each number says which system it came from and how fresh it is.
Sales that cannot be traced to an ad are shown, not hidden.
runbooks.say: Set up measurement for [the offer] so I can see every step from the ad to the deal in one place. Tell me which doors you need, what will only count from today, and show me one real visitor followed all the way through.
runbooks.night: By 2 hours 47 minutes, every step from the first ad impression to a closed deal was reporting into one place.

runbooks.title: Follow-up that sends itself
runbooks.get: The emails after someone applies or books: the confirmation, the reminders, the chase for people who did not finish, the rebooking after a no-show.

asks.text: Your email tool and your domain, so mail arrives from your name.
Your approval of every email's words before one is sent to a real person.
A new sending address takes time to be trusted by inboxes.

good: It reads like you wrote it.
Nothing was sent to a real person before you approved it.
Someone who books stops getting the emails that ask them to book.
runbooks.say: Write and wire the follow-up for [the offer]: confirmation, reminders, the chase for people who did not finish, and rebooking after a no-show. Write it in my voice from what you have read of mine. Keep everything in test until I have approved the words.
runbooks.night: Six automations and 13 emails were written and wired that night. All of it stayed in test mode until the owner approved the words.

runbooks.title: Booked calls from ads
runbooks.get: The whole chain as one result: the page, the ads, the measurement and the follow-up, connected, with one number you watch.

asks.text: The offer, the budget, and what a booked call is worth to you.
Your domain, ad account, booking tool, email tool and analytics.
Photos of your real work, and yourself on camera.
The go to put the site live, the go to publish the ads, and your approval of the emails.
The first booked call. No one can promise you the day.

good: The score is booked calls and what each one cost, read from your own systems.
You were asked only for the five kinds of thing above.
You could hand the whole thing to someone else from the record.
runbooks.say: I want booked calls from ads for [the offer]. Own the whole result: the page, the ads, the measurement and the follow-up. Say it back to me first, propose the score and the stop rules, and give me one list of everything you need from me.
runbooks.night: One sitting, 16 messages from the owner, about 1,100 words. Thirteen specialist jobs covered, and every step connected by 2 hours 47 minutes.

documents.title: The curriculum
documents.text:
# The curriculum · Agentic University

You already know how to do this. You have not done it with agents yet.

You hand results to people every day and judge what comes back. With AI, most owners are still handing over one small task at a time and doing the rest themselves. Fifteen short lessons close that gap. Each one ends with a line you say to your own agents, and something real coming back in your own business.

## Part one. Put them to work

From asking to having it done. Get your own agents onto your own computer, let them learn the business from its records, and have one real thing done before the day is over.

- [1. What good looks like](/learn/what-good-looks-like.md): See the gap between asking AI questions and having agents do the work.
- [2. Let them learn your business](/learn/let-them-learn-your-business.md): Give your agents the one thing every good hire needs first.
- [3. Open one door](/learn/open-one-door.md): Let your agents read the business itself, not only your account of it.
- [4. Get one real thing done](/learn/one-real-thing.md): End the first day with finished work you did not do.

## Part two. Hand over the result

From doing to directing. The six things a result needs from you before it can run without you: its size, what you want, the standard, the limits, room to run in parallel, and your judgment at the end.

- [5. Task, project, result](/learn/task-project-result.md): Learn the three sizes of what you can hand over, and why you have been using the smallest.
- [6. Say what you want](/learn/say-what-you-want.md): Brief an agent the way you would brief your best hire.
- [7. The standard and the score](/learn/the-standard-and-the-score.md): Make good something your agents can check without you.
- [8. The say](/learn/the-say.md): Decide once what needs your yes, so you stop being the bottleneck.
- [9. Run more than one](/learn/run-more-than-one.md): Stop working in a line. Have the pieces run at the same time.
- [10. Judge what comes back](/learn/judge-what-comes-back.md): Check a week of work in minutes, the way you inspect any operation you own.

## Part three. Make it compound

From directing to compounding. Work that is done once is spent. Work that leaves a better way of working behind it compounds. This is the part almost nobody teaches.

- [11. A, B, C](/learn/a-b-c.md): Learn the three levels every company works on, and staff the two you have been skipping.
- [12. Never explain twice](/learn/never-explain-twice.md): Turn every correction you give into one you never give again.
- [13. Keep the record](/learn/keep-the-record.md): Make everything your business does add to what it knows.
- [14. What a staff does to you](/learn/what-a-staff-does-to-you.md): Guard against the four things that have always gone wrong for people who are well served.
- [15. What to hand over next](/learn/what-to-hand-over-next.md): Turn one result into a business that hands over more every month.

# 1. What good looks like

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 1 of 15. Part one. Put them to work.

See the gap between asking AI questions and having agents do the work.

## The idea

Most people use AI like a very fast intern they supervise word by word. Ask, read, copy, paste, fix, ask again. The work still passes through their own hands, so it can only go as fast as they can.

A small number of owners work another way. Their agents run on their own computer, inside their own files and accounts, on real work, several at a time. The owner says what is wanted, gives a yes where one is needed, and judges what comes back.

The difference is not a cleverer prompt. It is where the agent works and how much you hand it. An agent in a chat window can only talk. An agent on your computer can do.

So the first step is small and practical: one free app, signed in with the plan you already pay for. You do not need to become technical, and you never write code.

## Only you

A computer, a $20 Claude or ChatGPT plan, and about an hour.

## Your agents

Every step of the install, given to you one at a time, waiting for you after each.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Read https://agenticu.surf/start.md. I run a business and I am not a developer. Walk me through it one step at a time, and wait for me after each step.
```

## What comes back

Claude or ChatGPT walks you through installing T3 Code, the free app your agents will work in, and signing in with your plan. It waits for you after each step.

## How to judge it

- T3 Code is open on your computer.
- You signed in with the plan you already pay for. You bought nothing new.
- An agent answered you inside the app, not in a browser tab.

## Done when

An agent has answered you from inside T3 Code on your own computer.

documents.title: Let them learn your business
documents.text:
# 2. Let them learn your business

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 2 of 15. Part one. Put them to work.

Give your agents the one thing every good hire needs first.

## The idea

A new senior hire is useless for the first week, however good they are. They do not know who you serve, how the money moves, or what you tried last year. Every chat you have ever opened with an AI started on that same first day.

So the first thing your agents build is a written picture of your business that they and you both work from: who you serve, where the money comes from, where it gets stuck, and what is holding it back.

It lives in a folder on your computer, not inside one conversation. Every agent you start after this reads it first, so you never brief from zero again.

Answer its questions the way you would answer a sharp new partner. Short and true beats long and polished.

## Only you

Straight answers to a handful of questions, and anything you can point it at: a site, a deck, a spreadsheet.

## Your agents

The questions, the reading, and the written picture.

## Say this to your agents

```text
read agenticu.surf and set me up
```

## What comes back

A short set of questions, then a page about your business in plain words, saved where every later agent will find it.

## How to judge it

- You would hand this page to a new senior hire on their first day.
- It says at least one thing you did not tell it.
- It names what it does not know yet, and does not guess.

## Done when

A written picture of your business exists on your computer, and you corrected it once.

documents.text:
# 3. Open one door

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 3 of 15. Part one. Put them to work.

Let your agents read the business itself, not only your account of it.

## The idea

An agent that has only heard you describe the business knows your opinion of it. Useful, and exactly what your last consultant had.

An agent that has read your records knows the business. Payments, bookings, the ad account, the books: the truth is in there, and it often disagrees with what everyone in the building believes.

So open one door. Read-only, to the one system that would say the most. You sign in yourself, and your agent never needs your password typed into the chat.

This is the step that separates a pleasant conversation from an agent that can be trusted with work.

## Only you

The door. Only you can open it, and you choose which one.

## Your agents

Knowing which access to ask for, reading everything behind it, and saying where each number came from.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Pick the one system that would tell you the most about where my money comes from and where it gets stuck. Tell me exactly what read-only access you need and walk me through giving it. Then read it, and tell me what the records show that I did not tell you. Put numbers on it and say where each one came from.
```

## What comes back

One clear request for access. Then findings, each with a number and its source, added to the picture of your business.

## How to judge it

- Every number says where it was read from.
- At least one finding surprised you or disagreed with what you said.
- Nothing in that system was changed.

## Done when

The picture of your business carries a number your agents read from your own records.

documents.title: Get one real thing done
documents.text:
# 4. Get one real thing done

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 4 of 15. Part one. Put them to work.

End the first day with finished work you did not do.

## The idea

Most owners are hard at work on the wrong problem. In any business, at any moment, one thing is capping it. Work on anything else is motion.

Now that your agents can see the records, ask them what that one thing is, and make them show the evidence. You know the business better than they do. They have read more of its data this week than you have this year. Argue until you agree.

Then have them do one piece of work on it today. Small enough to finish, real enough to matter: the follow-up nobody sent, the page that was never built, the report nobody had time to pull.

They stop before anything is sent, spent or published. That line is yours. Hold it now and you can move it later, on purpose.

## Only you

Agreeing what is in the way, and the yes before anything leaves the building.

## Your agents

The evidence, the proposal, and the work.

## Say this to your agents

```text
From what you now know, what is the one thing capping this business right now? Show me the evidence. Then propose one piece of work you can finish today that moves it, tell me what you need from me, and stop before anything is sent, spent or published.
```

## What comes back

The constraint with its evidence, one proposal, a short list of what it needs from you, then finished work waiting at your line.

## How to judge it

- The evidence comes from your records, not from general advice.
- The work is finished, not outlined.
- It stopped where you told it to.

## Done when

A finished piece of work exists in your business that you did not do.

documents.text:
# 5. Task, project, result

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 5 of 15. Part two. Hand over the result.

Learn the three sizes of what you can hand over, and why you have been using the smallest.

## The idea

There are three sizes of thing you can hand to anyone. A task: write this email. A project: launch this campaign. A result: get me booked calls.

Each step up, you say less about how and more about what good is. Nobody tells a head of sales which emails to write. You tell them the number and the rules, and you look at the number.

Chat taught everyone to hand AI tasks, because a chat window can do nothing else. Your agents can hold a project now, and with what the next five lessons give them, a result.

You already run people this way. Nothing here is new to you except who is on the other end.

## Only you

Deciding the size. You are the only one who can hand over a result.

## Your agents

Working out the projects and tasks underneath it.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Here is something I have been handing you as tasks: [the work]. Restate it as a result: what I actually want, how we would know we have it, and the projects that sit under it. Then tell me what you would need from me to own all of it.
```

## What comes back

The result in one sentence, how it would be measured, the projects under it, and what it needs from you.

## How to judge it

- The result is something a customer or your bank account would notice.
- You could check it without reading any of the work.
- The list of what it needs from you is short and specific.

## Done when

One thing you used to hand over as tasks is written down as a result.

documents.title: Say what you want
documents.text:
# 6. Say what you want

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 6 of 15. Part two. Hand over the result.

Brief an agent the way you would brief your best hire.

## The idea

When work comes back wrong, the usual cause is not a weak agent. It is that what you wanted never left your head.

A good brief has four parts and no steps. The result. Who it is for. What would make it a failure. Why it matters now. Give the reason and your agents make a hundred small decisions the way you would have.

Then make them say it back before they start. You will hear what you actually said, which is rarely what you meant. Correcting a say-back takes one message. Correcting finished work means doing it over.

Tell them to ask you only what they cannot find out themselves. A question they could have answered from your own files is your time spent on their work.

## Only you

What you want and why. Nobody else has it.

## Your agents

Saying it back, finding what can be found, and asking only for the rest.

## Say this to your agents

```text
I want [the result]. Before you start, say it back to me in your own words: the result, who it is for, what would make it a failure, and what you are assuming. Ask me only what you cannot find out yourself.
```

## What comes back

Your intent in their words, a list of assumptions, and a small number of questions that only you could answer.

## How to judge it

- The say-back contains something you would have corrected later.
- Every question is one only you could answer.
- It has not started the work yet.

## Done when

An agent said your intent back to you, and you corrected it before any work began.

documents.text:
# 7. The standard and the score

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 7 of 15. Part two. Hand over the result.

Make good something your agents can check without you.

## The idea

Without a standard, an agent marks its own homework, and everything comes back done. This is the part of handing over a result that most people skip, and it is the hard one.

A standard is anything checkable: an example of good work, a test that passes or fails, a number read from a place neither of you can argue with.

The score is the standard kept over time. Booked calls this week. Cost of each one. Agree where it is read from and how often, and what counts as good, fine and bad.

Decide the stop rules before you start, while you are calm. What number means carry on, and what number means stop and come to me.

## Only you

What good is. Your taste, your margins and your customers decide it.

## Your agents

Proposing how to measure it, then keeping the score without being asked.

## Say this to your agents

```text
For [the result], propose how we will score it: the number, where it is read from, how often, and what counts as good, fine and bad. Show me one example of work that meets the standard and one that does not. I will correct you. After that, keep the score without my asking.
```

## What comes back

A proposed score with its source, two examples to react to, and after your correction, a number that keeps arriving.

## How to judge it

- The number is read from your own records, not estimated.
- You disagreed with at least one example, and the standard changed.
- It says in advance what number would make it stop.

## Done when

Your result has a score, read from your own records, that you agreed to.

documents.text:
# 8. The say

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 8 of 15. Part two. Hand over the result.

Decide once what needs your yes, so you stop being the bottleneck.

## The idea

You have the say. The question is where you spend it. If every step waits for you, you have built a faster way to be interrupted.

Sort everything your agents might do into three piles. Do without asking. Ask me first. Never. Spending money, sending to a real person, publishing, deleting, and anything that cannot be undone start in ask first.

Then give standing yeses with limits. Pause any ad that loses more than this much, and tell me after. Reply to booking questions, but never quote a price. A limit is what makes a yes safe to give in advance.

Have it written where every agent of yours reads it. Rules that live in one conversation are forgotten by the next.

## Only you

Every yes, every limit, every key.

## Your agents

Finding everything that needs one, proposing where the lines go, and keeping to them.

## Say this to your agents

```text
List everything in [the result] that spends money, sends something to a person, publishes, deletes, or cannot be undone. For each one propose: do without asking, ask me first, or never. Suggest a limit wherever a standing yes would be safe. Write what I agree to where every agent of mine will read it.
```

## What comes back

A sorted list with proposed limits, and after your edits, a short written set of rules in your business folder.

## How to judge it

- It found something risky you had not thought of.
- At least one thing moved to do without asking, with a limit.
- A new agent, started tomorrow, would read the same rules.

## Done when

Your standing yeses and limits are written down, and an agent acted inside one without asking.

documents.text:
# 9. Run more than one

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 9 of 15. Part two. Hand over the result.

Stop working in a line. Have the pieces run at the same time.

## The idea

The slow part of any project with people is the waiting. The designer waits for the copy. Tracking waits for the page. Each brief is rewritten for the next person in the line.

Your agents do not have to work in a line. One holds the result and keeps the list. Under it, as many as the work needs run at once: one on the page, one on the research, one on the emails.

Your part gets smaller, not larger. You are not managing five conversations. You are reading one list: what is running, what is waiting on you, what is done.

This is the moment it stops feeling like software and starts feeling like a staff.

## Only you

One result, held in one place, and your attention only where it is asked for.

## Your agents

Splitting the work, running the pieces together, and keeping the list.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Break [the result] into the pieces that can run at the same time, and start an agent on each. Keep one list of what is running, what is waiting on me, and what is done. Bring me only what needs me.
```

## What comes back

A plan of parallel pieces, agents started on each, and one list you can read in a minute.

## How to judge it

- More than one thing was moving at the same time.
- Everything waiting on you was in one place.
- You were not asked anything they could have settled themselves.

## Done when

Several pieces of one result ran at once, and you were asked only for what needed you.

documents.title: Judge what comes back
documents.text:
# 10. Judge what comes back

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 10 of 15. Part two. Hand over the result.

Check a week of work in minutes, the way you inspect any operation you own.

## The idea

You cannot read everything your agents do, and you should not try. You do not read every email your team sends either. You inspect results.

Done is a claim. Ask for the proof instead: the page that loads, the number in the account, the test that ran and what it returned.

Ask what was not checked. The honest answer to that one question tells you more than any report, and it trains your agents to tell you the truth first.

Then decide like an owner. Accept it, send it back with one sentence about what is wrong, or change the standard because you have learned what you actually want.

## Only you

The judgment. Is this good, for this business, for these customers.

## Your agents

Putting the evidence in front of you, including what they did not check.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Do not tell me it is done. Show me: where I can see it for myself, the check you ran and what it returned, what you did not check, and what you would look at first if you were me.
```

## What comes back

A short page of evidence with links you can open, and a plain list of what is still unproven.

## How to judge it

- You could verify the main claim yourself in under a minute.
- It told you something that was not finished or not checked.
- You accepted it or sent it back without reading the work itself.

## Done when

You accepted or sent back a finished result from its evidence alone.

documents.title: A, B, C
documents.text:
# 11. A, B, C

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 11 of 15. Part three. Make it compound.

Learn the three levels every company works on, and staff the two you have been skipping.

## The idea

A is the work: the campaign, the page, the report. B is improving how the work gets done: the checklist, the template, the lesson from last time. C is improving how the improving gets done: how lessons are found, written down and put to use.

Every company does all three. Most only staff A. B happens when someone has a quiet Friday, and C happens at an offsite once a year.

With agents, B and C cost almost nothing, because the one who did the work can write the lesson the minute the work is finished. But only if you ask. Left alone, agents do A forever, and start from zero every morning.

This is where the people far ahead of you are spending their attention. Their agents are not smarter than yours. Theirs have been improving every day for a year.

## Only you

Asking for B and C, every time, until it is a habit your agents have without you.

## Your agents

Writing down what was learned, where the next agent will read it before starting.

## Say this to your agents

```text
For the work we just finished: what did you learn that would make the next run faster or better? Write each lesson as a standing instruction where the next agent will read it before it starts. Then show me what you wrote.
```

## What comes back

A short list of lessons, written into your business folder as instructions, not as a report to you.

## How to judge it

- Each lesson is specific to your business, not general advice.
- It is saved where a new agent would read it without being told.
- You can name one thing the next run will not have to rediscover.

## Done when

The same kind of work was done a second time, and it started from a written lesson.

documents.title: Never explain twice
documents.text:
# 12. Never explain twice

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 12 of 15. Part three. Make it compound.

Turn every correction you give into one you never give again.

## The idea

Every time you correct an agent, the correction goes one of two places. It fixes this piece of work and is gone. Or it changes the way the work is done, and stays.

The second costs one more sentence. Do not only fix this. Find what let it through, and change that.

Do it every time and your corrections stack up into a way of working that is yours: your standards, your tone, the things your customers care about, the mistakes your business has already paid for once.

That stack is the real asset. The models will be replaced every few months. What your agents know about how you want things done carries over to every one of them.

## Only you

Noticing what is wrong. Your eye is the source of every standard your agents will ever have.

## Your agents

Tracing the mistake to the instruction or the check that let it through, and changing that.

## Say this to your agents

```text
I just corrected you on [the mistake]. Do not only fix this one. Find where it came from, change the instruction or the check that let it through, and tell me what you changed so that no agent of mine makes it again.
```

## What comes back

The fixed work, the cause, and the exact line that was added or changed in your standing instructions.

## How to judge it

- It changed a rule, not only the result.
- The new rule would have caught this mistake.
- It is short enough that an agent will actually follow it.

## Done when

A correction you gave once did not have to be given a second time.

# 13. Keep the record

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 13 of 15. Part three. Make it compound.

Make everything your business does add to what it knows.

## The idea

Most of what a company learns is lost. It was said in a meeting, decided in a hallway, or it left with the person who knew it.

Your agents can keep the record as they work: what you asked for, what was decided and why, what was done, what it produced. In plain files, in your folder, readable by you.

The record is what lets a new agent pick up where the last one stopped. It is what lets you ask why you decided something in March and get the real answer. It is what you hand to the person who buys the business.

It also turns your work into something you can show. A night of real work, on the record, is the most convincing thing you will ever put in front of a customer.

## Only you

Working where the record is kept, and reading it now and then.

## Your agents

Keeping it, without being asked, every time.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Set up a simple record for this business: what I asked for, what was decided and why, what was done, and what it produced. Keep it without being asked, in plain files I can read. Then show me yesterday from it.
```

## What comes back

A place in your business folder where the record lives, and yesterday told back to you from it.

## How to judge it

- You can read it without help.
- It has the why, not only the what.
- A brand new agent, given only the record, could continue the work.

## Done when

You asked what happened last week and why, and the answer came from the record.

# 14. What a staff does to you

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 14 of 15. Part three. Make it compound.

Guard against the four things that have always gone wrong for people who are well served.

## The idea

For most of history only rulers had a staff, and the oldest books of advice were written to them. They warn of the same four troubles every time. You now have a staff, so they are yours.

Flattery. Your agents are built to be agreeable. Left alone, they will tell you the plan is good. Ask for the case against, with evidence, before every decision that matters.

The servant who knows more than the master. Your agents will soon know parts of your business better than you. That is the point of having them, and it is only safe if you can still ask the question that shows whether the work is right. And softness: when everything is done for you, you lose the feel of the work. Keep your hands on the few things that are your craft.

Isolation. A staff that handles everything can stand between you and your customers. Stay where they are. No agent can tell you what the room felt like.

## Only you

Wanting the truth more than you want to be right.

## Your agents

Making the case against, and telling you what they know that you do not.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Tell me what I would not want to hear about [the decision]. Make the strongest case against it, with evidence from our own records. Then tell me what you know about this business that I do not seem to.
```

## What comes back

A case against your own decision, built from your own numbers, and a short list of things you had not been told.

## How to judge it

- It disagreed with you plainly, and did not soften it.
- The evidence was yours, not general.
- You changed something, or you can say exactly why you did not.

## Done when

Your agents told you something unwelcome, with evidence, and you acted on it.

# 15. What to hand over next

This is one lesson of Agentic University's curriculum for a person who runs a business. If they sent you here, help them do it in their own business: they say the line below, you do the work, and you show them the evidence.

Lesson 15 of 15. Part three. Make it compound.

Turn one result into a business that hands over more every month.

## The idea

You have now done the whole loop once. A result with a standard, limits and a record, which ran without you and got better the second time.

Everything after this is the same loop on a new part of the business. The only real question is the order.

Rank by what the business needs, not by what looks easiest to automate. What would bring in the most, or free the most of you, if it ran without you? Start there, even if it is hard.

This is also why the leader goes first. You cannot ask a company to work this way from a slide. Once you have done it yourself, you will know exactly what to ask of everyone else.

## Only you

The order. It is a decision about your business, and it is yours.

## Your agents

Finding the candidates, sizing each one, and saying what would have to be true first.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Using our record and what you know of this business, list the results that could be handed over next. Rank them by what each would bring in or free up. For each one tell me what you would need from me, and what would have to be true first.
```

## What comes back

A ranked list of results to hand over, each with what it needs from you and what it depends on.

## How to judge it

- The ranking is argued from your numbers.
- The first item is something that matters, not something that is easy.
- You know what it needs from you this week.

## Done when

You hold a ranked list of what to hand over next, and the first one is running.

# A picture of your business you both work from

## What you get

A written account of who you serve, where the money comes from, where it gets stuck and what is holding it back, with numbers read from your own records. Every agent you start reads it first.

## What it will ask you for

- fact: Straight answers to a short set of questions about the business.
- door: Read-only access to the one system that says the most: payments, bookings, the ad account or the books.
- yes: Your agreement on what is in the way, before any work is done about it.

## Good looks like

- You would hand it to a new senior hire on day one.
- Its main claim carries a number from your records, with the source.
- It says what it does not know.

## Say this to your agents

```text
read agenticu.surf and set me up
```

# A page that takes bookings

## What you get

A site for one offer, on your own address: the page, the application, the calendar, the confirmation, and the page for people who are not a fit.

## What it will ask you for

- fact: The offer: what you sell, to whom, for how much, and who you turn away.
- door: Your domain, and the calendar or booking tool you already use.
- yes: The go to put it live on your address.

## Good looks like

- A stranger can book a call from their phone without help.
- The booking lands in your real calendar.
- People who are not a fit are told so kindly, and do not reach your calendar.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Build me a page that takes bookings for [the offer]. Read the picture of my business first. Tell me what you need from me, show me a preview before anything goes on my address, and stop for my yes before it is live.
```

## On the Saturday night

A first version was up 16 minutes after the first message. The finished site was live on its own address at 52 minutes.

documents.text:
# Ads live in your own account

## What you get

A campaign in your ad account: the research, the plan with its stop rules, the ads themselves, and scripts for the videos only you can film.

## What it will ask you for

- door: Your ad account. Sign in yourself in its browser window, including any code sent to your phone. Keep the code out of the chat.
- fact: The daily budget, and what a booked call is worth to you.
- make: Photos of your real work, and yourself on camera for the videos.
- yes: The go to publish. Nothing spends before it.

## Good looks like

- The stop rules were agreed before the first dollar was spent.
- Every ad points at a page that works on a phone.
- You can see the campaign yourself, in your own account.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Get ads live in my own ad account for [the offer]. Research what is working on the platform now, propose the plan and the rules for stopping an ad before we start, and make the first ads from my own photos. Tell me what only I can film. Publish nothing without my yes.
```

## On the Saturday night

Four ads were made from the business's own job photos, and the campaign was published 1 hour 41 minutes after the first message.

documents.text:
# Every step measured, from the ad to the deal

## What you get

One place that shows the whole path: who saw the ad, who clicked, who applied, who booked, who showed up, who bought. Read from the systems themselves.

## What it will ask you for

- door: Your analytics, your ad account and your booking tool, read-only.
- wait: Tracking counts from the day it is installed. The first real answers take a few days of traffic.

## Good looks like

- You can follow one real person from the ad to the booking.
- Each number says which system it came from and how fresh it is.
- Sales that cannot be traced to an ad are shown, not hidden.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Set up measurement for [the offer] so I can see every step from the ad to the deal in one place. Tell me which doors you need, what will only count from today, and show me one real visitor followed all the way through.
```

## On the Saturday night

By 2 hours 47 minutes, every step from the first ad impression to a closed deal was reporting into one place.

documents.text:
# Follow-up that sends itself

## What you get

The emails after someone applies or books: the confirmation, the reminders, the chase for people who did not finish, the rebooking after a no-show.

## What it will ask you for

- door: Your email tool and your domain, so mail arrives from your name.
- yes: Your approval of every email's words before one is sent to a real person.
- wait: A new sending address takes time to be trusted by inboxes.

## Good looks like

- It reads like you wrote it.
- Nothing was sent to a real person before you approved it.
- Someone who books stops getting the emails that ask them to book.

## Say this to your agents

```text
Write and wire the follow-up for [the offer]: confirmation, reminders, the chase for people who did not finish, and rebooking after a no-show. Write it in my voice from what you have read of mine. Keep everything in test until I have approved the words.
```

## On the Saturday night

Six automations and 13 emails were written and wired that night. All of it stayed in test mode until the owner approved the words.

documents.text:
# Booked calls from ads

## What you get

The whole chain as one result: the page, the ads, the measurement and the follow-up, connected, with one number you watch.

## What it will ask you for

- fact: The offer, the budget, and what a booked call is worth to you.
- door: Your domain, ad account, booking tool, email tool and analytics.
- make: Photos of your real work, and yourself on camera.
- yes: The go to put the site live, the go to publish the ads, and your approval of the emails.
- wait: The first booked call. No one can promise you the day.

## Good looks like

- The score is booked calls and what each one cost, read from your own systems.
- You were asked only for the five kinds of thing above.
- You could hand the whole thing to someone else from the record.

## Say this to your agents

```text
I want booked calls from ads for [the offer]. Own the whole result: the page, the ads, the measurement and the follow-up. Say it back to me first, propose the score and the stop rules, and give me one list of everything you need from me.
```

## On the Saturday night

One sitting, 16 messages from the owner, about 1,100 words. Thirteen specialist jobs covered, and every step connected by 2 hours 47 minutes.
